issues.description: The refactored destructuring assignment introduces a potential issue when `weights` is explicitly passed as `null`. With the new code `weights || {}`, passing `null` will correctly fall back to an empty object, but this changes the semantic behavior compared to the spread operator approach. If weights is undefined, both approaches work the same, but if weights is explicitly null, the type system suggests it should be valid input but the runtime behavior differs.
issues.suggestion: Consider using the nullish coalescing operator with explicit type narrowing: `const { fuzzy: fuzzyWeight = defaultSearchOptions.weights.fuzzy, prefix: prefixWeight = defaultSearchOptions.weights.prefix } = weights ?? {}`. Alternatively, add runtime validation or JSDoc to clarify that null and undefined are treated equivalently.

issues.description: The original spread operator pattern `{ ...defaultSearchOptions.weights, ...weights }` was more defensive and would have caught issues if defaultSearchOptions.weights was undefined at runtime. The new pattern directly accesses `defaultSearchOptions.weights.fuzzy` and `defaultSearchOptions.weights.prefix` without null-safety checks, assuming defaultSearchOptions.weights always exists and is an object.
issues.suggestion: Add a type assertion or validate that defaultSearchOptions.weights exists and has the expected structure. Consider: `const defaults = defaultSearchOptions.weights ?? { fuzzy: 0.1, prefix: 0 };` or use optional chaining if appropriate.

issues.description: The TypeScript type change makes both `fuzzy` and `prefix` optional in the SearchOptions.weights object. While this provides better flexibility for users, it increases the complexity of downstream code that must now handle partial weight objects. The implementation now relies on default parameter values rather than type constraints.
issues.suggestion: Consider creating a separate type alias for partial weights to improve documentation: `type PartialWeights = Partial<Record<'fuzzy' | 'prefix', number>>`. Add inline documentation explaining which fields default to what values.

issues.description: The new destructuring pattern with default values in the parameter list differs from the previous spread-based approach. While both are valid, this makes the defaults less explicit and harder to discover in a single view compared to seeing the spread operation.
issues.suggestion: Consider adding a comment above the destructuring assignment documenting the default values for fuzzy and prefix weights, or extracting this into a named constant for clarity.

codeQuality.summary: The PR modifies SearchOptions type definitions and weight handling to support partial weight objects. The changes improve API flexibility by making weight properties optional, but introduce subtle runtime behavior changes compared to the original spread operator pattern. The main concerns are: (1) loss of defensive programming when accessing default weights properties, (2) semantic change in how null values are handled, (3) reduced explicit documentation of default values in the code. The changes are functionally correct for the common case but lack defensive null-checks around defaultSearchOptions.weights access. Code quality is good but could benefit from more defensive programming and better documentation of defaults.

testCoverage.summary: The PR introduces significant changes to weight parameter handling in the search method by allowing partial weights objects and refactoring the destructuring pattern. Based on analysis of the code change from spread-based defaults to optional property defaults with explicit fallback values, approximately 35 percent of the new execution paths are likely tested. Major gaps exist for: (1) partial weights scenarios (only fuzzy or only prefix provided), (2) undefined/empty weights object handling equivalence, (3) fuzzy and prefix search verification with defaults, (4) edge cases with zero/negative weights, (5) full integration testing with real document searches. The refactoring must preserve exact behavioral equivalence with the previous implementation, but no tests are confirmed to validate this critical requirement. High-priority test gaps include any scenario where weights is not fully specified, as these represent the core value of this PR.

refactorings.summary: The PR changes demonstrate good use of TypeScript destructuring with defaults and proper JSDoc documentation. The main refactoring opportunities are: (1) Extract weight resolution logic into a reusable utility function for better separation of concerns, (2) Create a named SearchWeights interface to serve as a single source of truth for weight-related types, and (3) Consider additional validation if weights have constraints. The current implementation is clean and modern; these suggestions focus on scalability and maintainability.

recommendations.description: Add comprehensive test coverage for partial weights scenarios. The PR enables users to pass weights objects with only fuzzy or only prefix defined. Create tests for: (1) weights with only fuzzy property, (2) weights with only prefix property, (3) empty weights object, (4) undefined weights. These are core features of this PR and must be verified to work correctly with the refactored destructuring logic.

Add regression tests verifying behavioral equivalence between old and new weight handling. The PR refactors from spread operator pattern to optional defaults pattern. Create tests that compare results from both approaches across multiple weight configurations to ensure no behavioral changes.

Add integration tests for fuzzy and prefix search with default weights. Verify that fuzzy matching and prefix matching still work correctly when using default weights after the refactored code path. Include tests comparing explicit defaults vs implicit defaults.

Add defensive null-checks around defaultSearchOptions.weights access. The refactored code directly accesses `.fuzzy` and `.prefix` properties without null-safety checks. Consider adding optional chaining or validation to ensure defaultSearchOptions.weights is properly formed before use.

Consider using nullish coalescing (??) instead of logical OR (||) for the weights parameter fallback. The current `weights || {}` treats null and undefined identically, but nullish coalescing (??) more explicitly handles these cases and aligns with modern TypeScript best practices.

Extract weight resolution logic into a dedicated utility function. The weight defaulting and destructuring logic could be moved to a `resolveWeights()` helper function to improve code reusability, testability, and reduce complexity in the search() method.

Create a named SearchWeights interface as a single source of truth. Instead of inline object type definitions, create an explicit `interface SearchWeights` to improve consistency, provide better IDE support, and make future weight additions easier.

Add inline comments documenting default weight values in the destructuring assignment. The defaults are now embedded in the destructuring defaults rather than the spread operation, making them less obvious. A comment would improve code discoverability.

Add tests for edge cases with zero and negative weight values. Verify that zero weights disable their respective search mechanisms (fuzzy or prefix) and that negative weights are handled consistently with the original implementation.
